extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing secondary considerations (commercial success, long‑felt need, copying, skepticism, etc.) in the patent nonobviousness/obviousness analysis during prosecution and related proceedings. Focuses on evidentiary burdens, nexus, scope, and evidentiary weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages Disclosed or Inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. Therefore, evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence and arguments rebutting a §103 rejection need not be contained within the specification; such evidence presented during ex parte prosecution is part of the totality of the record (In re Chu). Examples include inherent properties (In re Zenitz) and undisclosed relative toxicity (Ex parte Sasajima). The specification need not disclose proportions or values as critical for applicants to present evidence showing such proportions/values are critical (In re Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Production for Evidence of Commercial Success and Nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who is asserting commercial success to support its contention of nonobviousness bears the burden of proof in establishing commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO relies on applicants to provide hard evidence of commercial success because the Office lacks resources to gather such evidence. The term 'nexus' denotes a factually and legally sufficient connection between the commercial success evidence and the claimed invention so the evidence is probative of nonobviousness (see In re Huang; Demaco Corp. v. F. Von Langsdorff Licensing Ltd.). See MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145 for guidance on assessing nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Abroad is Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success abroad, as well as in the United States, is relevant in resolving the issue of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign sales can be probative of commercial success (Lindemann Maschinenfabrik GMBH v. American Hoist & Derrick Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Commensurate in Scope With Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness including commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of commercial success must be due to claimed features and not to unclaimed features (In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies Inc. v. Manbeck). Evidence limited to narrower embodiments or features recited only in dependent claims may not be commensurate with broader independent claims. See MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145 for nexus guidance. A generic affidavit phrase saying a product was 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' is insufficient to establish nexus (Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements When Claimed Invention Is Not Coextensive With Commercial Product or Process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular range is claimed, applicant does not need to show commercial success at every point in the range; evidence at typical points can be persuasive if affidavits indicate operation throughout the claimed ranges approximates that at the commercial point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the commercially successful product is not coextensive with the claimed invention, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product (In re Hollingsworth; Demaco). Affidavits indicating typical operation across ranges can support commensurateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Must Be Attributable to the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success alleged must be shown to be a result of the invention claimed, not the result of heavy promotion, advertising, shifts in advertising, purchaser ties to the applicant/assignee, blocking patents, or other extraneous business events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions or opinions by inventors as to purchaser motivation are entitled to little weight (In re Mageli; In re Noznick). Licensing may be of limited evidentiary value if driven by business reasons unrelated to unobviousness. Market-entry preclusion by blocking patents can weaken the inference from commercial success (UCB, Inc. v. Actavis Labs. UT, Inc.). Compare civil litigation evidentiary standards where proving a negative is not required (Demaco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Must Flow From Functions and Advantages Disclosed or Inherent in the Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, the commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success attributable to improvements/modifications by others is not pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show the success results from the invention's disclosed/inherent advantages (In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.; Merck & Cie v. Gnosis S.P.A.). If success results from a 'unique combination' or synergistic interaction not recited in the claims, nexus may be lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus Establishment in Design Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a nexus between commercial success and the claimed invention is especially difficult in design cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of commercial success in design patents must be clearly attributable to the design itself and not to brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors; lack of such attribution undermines probative value (Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales Figures Must Be Adequately Defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures do not show commercial success absent evidence as to market share, the time period of sales, or what sales would normally be expected in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales numbers require context (market share, timeframe, expected baseline) to be probative (Cable Electric Products, Inc. v. Genmark, Inc.; Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑Felt Need and Failure of Others
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must satisfy a long‑felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not solved by others; establishing long‑felt need requires objective evidence that an art‑recognized problem existed for a long period without solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three factors: (1) the need must have been recognized by those of ordinary skill (In re Gershon); (2) the need must not have been satisfied by another before the inventor's invention (Newell Companies v. Kenney Mfg. Co.); (3) the invention must actually satisfy the long‑felt need (In re Cavanagh). The absence of recognition of the problem by the art undermines a long‑felt‑need claim (Gershon). See Ex parte Thompson (informative) for Board analysis reversing obviousness based on long‑felt need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑Felt Need Is Measured From Date Problem Identified and Efforts Are Made
rubrics_metrics.description: Long‑felt need is analyzed as of the date the problem is identified and articulated, and when there is evidence of efforts to solve it — not as of the date of the most pertinent prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing for assessing long‑felt need is tied to identification of the problem and documented efforts to solve it (Texas Instruments Inc. v. Int’l Trade Comm’n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Factors Contributing to Presence of Long‑Felt Need
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to solve a long‑felt need may be due to lack of interest or lack of appreciation of an invention’s potential or marketability rather than want of technical know‑how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider market/regulatory context or lack of appreciation; sworn affidavits by a bona fide licensee can add weight if the license is arm’s length (Scully Signal Co. v. Electronics Corp. of America; Environmental Designs, Ltd. v. Union Oil Co. of Cal.; In re Tiffin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of Experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief by experts constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism expressed before inventors proved experts wrong, and sustained research efforts preceding the invention, can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness (Environmental Designs v. Union Oil; In re Dow Chemical Co.; Burlington Industries Inc. v. Quigg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors are copying the invention rather than using the prior art may be presented as secondary evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying requires evidence of efforts to replicate a specific product (internal documents, disassembly, photographs used as blueprint) or access to confidential disclosure plus substantial similarity (Wyers v. Master Lock; Iron Grip Barbell Co. v. USA Sports; Liqwd, Inc. v. L’Oreal). Copying is persuasive when an alleged infringer expended substantial time/effort failing to design independently and then copied. Mere copying is insufficient if attributable to other factors (lack of concern for patents, contempt) or if the copy is not identical and the other manufacturer did not expend great effort (Cable Electric; Pentec; Vandenberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability of References
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not express opinions on the operability of a patent; affidavits/declarations attacking operability must rebut the presumption of operability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent is presumed operable; a showing that it is possible to operate within the disclosure without obtaining the alleged product does not overcome the presumption (Metropolitan Eng. Co. v. Coe; In re Sasse; In re Weber). Skilled artisans are presumed to make routine experiments/adaptations. Failures by uninterested experimenters carry little weight (In re Michalek; In re Reid). Alleged inoperability of non‑relied features leaves the rest of the reference effective (In re Shepherd). A patentee’s declaration that the reference was not intended to be used as claimed is immaterial (In re Pio), but typographical error admissions can be persuasive (In re Yale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and Operability of Applicant’s Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when it is proper to require evidence of utility or operativeness for applicant’s disclosure and how to evaluate such evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2107.02 and §§2107–2107.03 for utility examination guidelines and legal precedent relevant to the utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101; use those standards when deciding whether to require evidence of utility/operability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of Disclosure (Enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether the specification provides an enabling disclosure in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once examiner establishes a prima facie lack of enablement, the burden shifts to applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention from the disclosure (In re Brandstadter). Evidence supplementing a deficient specification must establish that the missing information would have been known to those skilled in the art (In re Howarth). Affidavits/declarations are not acceptable to establish facts the specification should recite (In re Buchner; In re Smyth). Opinion testimony that merely asserts disclosure is of limited weight, but expert testimony that explains the factual basis for an opinion may be helpful and is evaluated case‑by‑case (In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution Affidavit or Declaration to Overcome Rejection Under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances an affidavit or declaration may be submitted to attribute an activity, a reference, or part of a reference to the inventor to overcome a rejection based on pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unequivocal declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 by an inventor that they conceived or invented subject matter disclosed but not claimed in the reference can be sufficient if corroborated (In re DeBaun). Documentation contemporaneous with conception/invention and declarations by other inventors may corroborate inventorship (EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen). When the reference is a U.S. patent or application publication containing claims relied upon in the rejection, a 37 CFR 1.132 declaration must also explain the presence of any additional inventor in the reference (e.g., explain joint inventorship of other claims). This section is not applicable to first‑inventor‑to‑file AIA applications except as noted for pre‑AIA 102(g) (see related MPEP sections).
